extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, government officials, and engineers dealing with navigable-waters regulation (Secretary of War, Chief of Engineers, harbor/river authorities)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules governing bridges, piers, wharves, harbor lines, permits, notices, hearings, and enforcement under U.S. navigable-waters statutes (acts of 1888, 1890, 1899, etc.), as applied by the Secretary of War and Chief of Engineers. Covers when permits may issue, what notices must contain, hearing rights, scope of discretion, and limits on remedies (military force, revocation, receivership).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific statutory authority required for transfer of rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Transfers of rights (e.g., to a corporation) confer no right of transfer unless there is specific authority of statute for the purpose; otherwise the transfer, if assumed, will be ineffectual and void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites authorities and dates; emphasizes that statutory grant is necessary before a purported transfer can be effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of plans from party in possession or control
rubrics_metrics.description: Plans for reconstruction, renewal, reconstruction, or repair of a bridge will be accepted from the person or corporation in actual possession or control of the property — presumption being that such possession or control is legal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies where franchise passed with title after plans approved and bridge built; supports acting on plans from current occupant rather than remote claimants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of franchise and user rights for wagon vs railroad ways
rubrics_metrics.description: A bridge belonging to the United States may be both wagon and railroad bridge; the railroad company has no authority over the wagon way and cannot prevent third parties from using the wagon way unless expressly authorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Merchants' Bridge (Rock Island–Davenport) — United States control subject to limited railroad right-of-way conditions (certain freight excluded).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice-and-hearing requirement before requiring alteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Before notice to alter a bridge is given, the person owning or controlling it is entitled, under the act of 1890, section 4, to be heard on the changes specified and on the time for making them; absent such opportunity to be heard, the party will not be liable to the penalties of section 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple decisions (C. 798; 1511; 14832) cited; hearing covers both substance of required changes and schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice must specify the changes required
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice to be given to the person or corporation owning or controlling an obstructing bridge 'shall specify the changes required to be made', and the party must be given a 'reasonable opportunity to be heard.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under act of Sept. 19, 1890 (section 4); later holdings construe 'specify' to mean specifying changes recommended by Chief of Engineers (see IV A discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary's determination of obstruction is judicial in nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The power vested in the Secretary of War by section 4 of the act of Sept. 19, 1890, to determine whether a bridge is an obstruction to navigation is judicial, not merely ministerial; it vests him with specific discretion and is for him alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus cannot be exercised by Assistant Secretary; should involve adjudicative elements (hearings, findings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary limited to requiring structural changes recommended by Chief of Engineers
rubrics_metrics.description: Under section 18 of the act of March 3, 1899, in giving notice the Secretary 'shall specify the changes recommended by the Chief of Engineers that are required to be made,' and he has no authority to require other or additional structural changes than those so recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision G. 22317, Apr. 15, 1909; distinguishes Secretary's discretion on jurisdiction from duty to require only the Chief's recommended structural modifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceedings to alter may not be initiated before bridge is an actual obstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice to alter must be given when the bridge 'is' an unreasonable obstruction; the Secretary cannot initiate proceedings on the ground the bridge will obstruct at some future time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of future increases in commerce when prescribing alterations
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining the character of required alterations, anticipated future increases of commerce on a stream may be considered and the required changes should have such probable future requirements in view as well as present commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in railway bridge/Pablo Creek (G. 22317, Aug. 28, 1908); customary to take into account probable future navigational needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strictness and precision of notice where criminal liability may follow
rubrics_metrics.description: Because notice to alter (act of 1890, section 4) is preliminary to fixing criminal liability, such notice should be strict and precise: identify the bridge and owner, and 'specify fully the change or changes required' (height, width of span/draw, etc.), and show a reasonable opportunity to be heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P. 43, 431, Nov., 1890; G. 14832, June 24, 1903; emphasizes specificity to support later prosecutions or penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeal of prior statutory procedure requires new notice under current statute
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings begun under a prior statute (act of 1888) that has been repealed cannot result in prosecution; a new notice under the existing statute must be given and proceedings commenced de novo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P. 43, 431, Nov., 1890; 49, 72, Sept., 1891; criminal liability cannot be based on expired penal act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different enforcement authorities depending on obstruction type
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the act of 1890, section 4, the Secretary of War must notify the district attorney only in case of alterations not made or completed bridges; as to other obstructions the duty to enforce devolves upon the 'officers and agents' specified in section 11.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P. 52, 343, Mar., 1892 — distinguishes procedural path depending on nature of obstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for alterations where property has passed to a receiver
rubrics_metrics.description: If, after notice to alter, the bridge company has failed and property has passed to a receiver, the proper method is to move the court that appointed the receiver to order the receiver to make the alteration; neither owner nor receiver can be made personally amenable without such court order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P. 37, 361, Jan., 1890; P. 60, 118, June, 1893; courts control receivers' authority to incur expense for alterations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approval of previously approved plans does not preclude future required alterations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where plans of a bridge had been approved without reserving the right to require changes, sections 4 and 5 of the act of Sept. 19, 1890, nevertheless vest the Secretary with jurisdiction to require future changes in any bridge 'now constructed or which may be hereafter constructed' so that the bridge when altered may not be 'an unreasonable obstruction' — approval is subject to future necessary alterations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 27747, Feb. 13, 1911; approval without reservation does not bar later required modifications to keep navigation free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Owners may waive hearing and submit plans; Secretary's approval prescribes alterations
rubrics_metrics.description: If owners waive hearing and notice and submit plans of alterations, the Secretary may approve those plans; his approval effectively prescribes that the bridge be altered as indicated by the approved plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 1157, Mar., 1895; 24, 818, May 7, 1909 — procedural alternate to notice/hearing when owners voluntarily submit plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary may not use military force to effect removal/alteration of obstructions
rubrics_metrics.description: The acts providing for removal of obstructions by requiring alteration of bridges do not empower the Secretary of War to resort to military force; execution of provisions is left to law officers and the courts, and the Secretary must inform the Attorney General to institute proceedings when owners neglect to alter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P. 44, 85, July, 1890; emphasizes legal/court enforcement rather than executive military action.

rubrics_metrics.name: No statutory authority to authorize temporary closing of drawbridge for repairs (but department practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no U.S. statute expressly empowering the Secretary of War to authorize closing a drawbridge during repairs, but the War Department may advise applicants that it will not take action regarding the bridge as an obstruction during necessary repairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 3299, June 1897 — administrative accommodation without explicit statutory grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permits under section 10 (Mar. 3, 1899) required for structures in navigable waters outside harbor lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 10 makes unlawful construction of wharves, piers, etc., in navigable waters outside established harbor lines except on plans recommended by the Chief of Engineers and authorized by the Secretary of War; a permit confers no franchise or interest in shore/bed but is a condition precedent relating to commerce and navigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 8360, June, 1900; C. 21193, Feb. 12, 1907; permits do not override state or local laws or private rights and cannot issue until Chief of Engineers has approved/recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form, limits, and revocability of permits are within Secretary's discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 10 does not limit the Secretary's discretion as to the character/form of permits; permission may be formal or by letter, may be revocable at will, limited as to amount, season, river condition, and may impose notice conditions on subtakers/assignees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 27899, Nov. 7–8, 1911; examples include piers, booms, ferry cables, pipe lines; permits may include conditions and notice requirements for assignees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riparian owners' rights subordinate to federal regulation of navigable capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Riparian owners' rights under State law as to use of a navigable stream are subject to the paramount authority of the United States to regulate; withdrawals may be prohibited if they injure the navigable capacity of the stream.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 27899, Nov. 7–8, 1911; federal permit regime can limit state-law riparian privileges when navigation affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation vs. approval: Secretary's approval may be communicated by Chief of Engineers for routine matters
rubrics_metrics.description: While discretionary duties are generally not delegable, approval by the Secretary of War may be implemented by having the Chief of Engineers communicate that approval to applicants for routine structures (booms, weirs, fish traps, dredging approaches, cables, pipelines), so long as the action is not a forbidden delegation of discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 16336 (May 13, 1904; Nov. 19, 1910; Feb. 18, 1911); contrasted with cases where delegating discretionary decision-making (e.g., local engineer to permit pile-driving in Newport Harbor) was improper (C. 7767, Mar. 7 & 15, 1900).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary may require applicant to show authority to construct if not shore owner
rubrics_metrics.description: When an applicant who is not an owner of shore property applies for permission to place an advertising sign off the coast, the Secretary may properly require, as a condition precedent, a showing that the applicant is authorized to construct the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 26678, May 9, 1910 — protects against permitting structures by persons lacking franchise/shore rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local/regional bodies' jurisdiction subject to Secretary/Chief for work outside harbor lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdiction of local authorities (e.g., Commissioners of District of Columbia) under wharf acts is to be exercised subject to authority conferred on the Secretary of War and Chief of Engineers for work outside harbor lines; such applications should be submitted for recommendation/authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 13900, May 27, 1903 — ensures federal oversight when work affects federal harbor lines/navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary empowered to authorize laying of mains and similar works across channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Under river and harbor appropriation acts (e.g., July 13, 1892), the Secretary of War was empowered to authorize laying of a water main across the bed of the channel of any navigable water of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P. 65, 352, June, 1894; used as basis for licenses/permissions for utilities crossing navigable channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of weirs/booms in navigable waters unlawful without Secretary authority when detrimental
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction, without authority of the Secretary of War, of weirs or other structures in navigable waters outside established harbor lines (or where none established) is unlawful when they will be detrimental to navigation; local town licenses do not excuse such violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P. 53, 45, Apr., 1892; P. 58, 347, Mar., 1893 — applies to fish weirs and booms that obstruct navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on depositing ballast/refuse in certain harbors is penal and strictly construed
rubrics_metrics.description: Act of Aug. 17, 1894 (sec. 6) prohibits discharging/depositing ballast, refuse, dirt, etc., in waters of any harbor or river for whose improvement Congress appropriated money, and as a penal statute must be strictly construed, not generally extended to tributaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 581, Oct., 1894; C. 21290, Nov. 14, 1907; however, other holdings: dumping in Lake Michigan causing shoaling may violate sec. 3 of July 13, 1892 (C. 1537, July 24, 1895).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic or distance limits affect applicability of dumping prohibitions and sanitary designations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some prohibitions (e.g., dumping ballast) were held not enforceable beyond the 3-mile limit in New York Harbor; the harbor supervisor, with Secretary approval, may designate deposit places beyond 3 miles to protect navigation and sanitation of adjacent coasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P. 51, 154, Dec., 1891; C. 20031, July 11, 1906 — recognizes limits of police jurisdiction and allowance for sanitary protective designations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies cannot grant exclusive privileges over public navigable resources
rubrics_metrics.description: No executive department can give private parties the exclusive privilege of harvesting natural products (e.g., ice) from any part of a navigable river of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 1817, Nov., 1895 — prevents exclusive grants by executive branch over common navigable resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal authorization required to remove/modify state structures affecting navigable capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Removal or modification of state dams that would change the capacity of a navigable river may be unlawful without proper authorization of the Secretary of War upon favorable recommendation of the Chief of Engineers under section 10 of March 3, 1899.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 14235, Mar. 25, 1903 — demonstrates federal control where state action affects interstate navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty and statute interaction: later treaty supplants earlier statute for certain diversions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a later treaty (e.g., Jan. 11, 1909) conflicts with an earlier statute (act of June 29, 1906), the treaty replaces the statute in conflicting incidents; licenses under the earlier act expire per their terms and future action is governed by treaty provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 19094, Jan. 11, 1911 — example regarding diversion from the Niagara River and appointment/expenses of commissioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harbor lines should be located as near shore as reasonable navigational demands allow
rubrics_metrics.description: Harbor lines should be kept as near to the shore as reasonable present or prospective demands of navigation may require, because once established and structures begun it is difficult to move lines further toward the shore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: a. 28243, Apr. 29, 1911 — planning principle to minimize future conflicts and reclamation difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: In establishing harbor lines, littoral owners' vested rights must be recognized though regulated
rubrics_metrics.description: When establishing harbor lines under section 12 of the act of Sept. 19, 1890, the Secretary may prescribe regulations under which littoral owners' vested rights (property in flats, wharf/dock out to channel) are recognized and protected; he may regulate building out but cannot prohibit or condemn their property; his authority is limited to what is necessary for protection of interstate navigation, not mere local traffic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P. 52, 211, Feb., 1892; P. 51, 132, Dec., 1891 — balances federal navigation interests with private property rights of littoral owners.
